title: Newborn sepsis with low glucose
objective: Name maternal, neonatal and treatment-related risk factors for neonatal sepsis, and recognize its subtle signs, including hypothermia rather than fever
secondaryObjectives: Obtain adequate-volume blood cultures and give empiric ampicillin with an aminoglycoside promptly, knowing cephalosporins alone miss Listeria
Recognize neonatal hypoglycemia (jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, seizures), start early feeding, and give IV dextrose when needed
Explain how cold stress causes hypoglycemia, acidosis and hypoxemia, and rewarm using skin-to-skin contact, radiant warmers or incubators

sources.note: Primary text read 2026-11-11 (a hosted PDF of the clinical report): pediatric culture bottles 'generally require a minimum inoculum of 1 mL of blood'; 'Ampicillin and gentamicin, in combination, is the first choice for empirical therapy for EOS'; suspected intraamniotic infection is a single maternal intrapartum temperature of 39.0 C or more, or 38.0-38.9 C persisting more than 30 minutes, plus another sign; the categorical algorithm counts ROM over 18 hours; CSF culture ideally before antibiotics in the highest-risk infants, but not if it would compromise the infant. The report sets no minute count for the first dose.

sources.cite: UCSF Benioff Children's Hospitals. Screening and Management of Hypoglycemia in Late Preterm and Term Infants >=34 weeks GA (clinical pathway, based on the AAP 2011 clinical report, Adamkin DH, Pediatrics 2011;127(3):575-579)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11. The AAP 2011 report itself was not opened; its values are as relayed by this pathway: concerning signs (seizure, lethargy, hypotonia, apnea, cyanosis) with glucose below 45 mg/dL get IV treatment; at 4-24 h the AAP threshold for asymptomatic infants is below 35 with a target above 45; IV bolus D10W 2-3 mL/kg; then D10W at 80 mL/kg/day (3.5 mL/kg/h), a glucose infusion rate of 5.5 mg/kg/min; recheck 30 minutes after a symptomatic IV intervention.

brief.situation: 08:00, admission to the NICU from the mother-baby unit. A girl born at 39 weeks, 3.4 kg, now 8 hours old. Her mother is GBS positive and had one dose of ampicillin shortly before delivery, which the obstetric team recorded as inadequate prophylaxis; membranes were ruptured for 20 hours; maternal temperature 38.4 for an hour in labor.
handover: Fed poorly at 06:00 and refused at 07:30. The nurse found her jittery and cool to the touch.
Axillary temperature 36.1, HR 176, RR 68, SpO2 96% in room air. No glucose has been checked since birth.
No IV yet. The neonatal nurse practitioner is on the unit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Results and procedures take minutes; you can skip ahead while you wait, and the skip stops at an alarm or a result.
Medications need the nurse practitioner's order; call with an SBAR.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at the three-hour review, then a debrief scores what you did.

whatNow.question: What do you think is happening to this baby, and what do you do first?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Names possible early-onset sepsis from the risk factors (GBS with inadequate prophylaxis, ROM over 18 h, maternal intrapartum fever) and the subtle signs (hypothermia rather than fever, poor feeding, jitteriness, tachycardia), plus symptomatic hypoglycemia worsened by cold stress.
parts.modelAnswer: Early-onset sepsis until proven otherwise: GBS-positive mother with inadequate prophylaxis, 20 hours of ruptured membranes and a maternal fever, and a baby who is cool rather than febrile, feeding poorly, jittery and tachycardic. The glucose is low and she has symptoms, and cold stress is burning more of it.

parts.label: What first
parts.criteria: Warms her; treats symptomatic hypoglycemia with IV dextrose (bolus then infusion) rather than feeds alone, and rechecks in about 30 min; draws a blood culture of at least 1 mL then gives ampicillin and gentamicin promptly; escalates with an SBAR.
parts.modelAnswer: Warmer on, call the nurse practitioner, IV in. Symptomatic low glucose needs IV dextrose, a 2 mL/kg D10 bolus then an infusion, and a recheck in 30 minutes, not just a feed. A 1 mL blood culture, then ampicillin and gentamicin without delay.

expertPath.text: Warmer on, glucose check, assess: cool, jittery, tachycardic, poor feeding, with three sepsis risk factors. Call the nurse practitioner naming sepsis and low glucose. Start an IV.
Glucose 31 with symptoms: IV dextrose, not a feed. Gel can bridge while the IV goes in.
IV in: D10W 2 mL/kg, then 80 mL/kg/day. Blood culture of at least 1 mL, then ampicillin and gentamicin.
Recheck the glucose 30 min after the bolus. Keep warming to 36.5-37.5.

seizure.headline: Hypoglycemic seizure
seizure.body: A jittery, poorly feeding baby with a low glucose has symptomatic hypoglycemia: IV dextrose, not a feed. Find when the glucose was first checked and when IV dextrose started.

collapse.headline: Collapse in septic shock
collapse.body: The risk factors and the subtle signs were there at 08:00. Find when the culture and the antibiotics went in.

stable.headline: Stabilized on time
stable.body: Warmth, IV dextrose for symptomatic hypoglycemia with an infusion and a recheck, a proper culture and ampicillin with gentamicin inside the hour. That is the expert path.

stableLate.headline: Stabilized, by a slower route
stableLate.body: She is better, but check the dextrose timing, whether the culture came first, the antibiotic choice and time, and when she was warmed.

time_up.headline: Still low or cold
time_up.body: Glucose and temperature are basics that keep injuring a septic newborn until they are fixed.

scoring.modelReasoning: A term newborn with three risk factors for early-onset sepsis (GBS colonization with inadequate prophylaxis, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal intrapartum fever) presenting with subtle signs: hypothermia rather than fever, poor feeding, jitteriness and tachycardia. Her glucose is low and she is symptomatic, so she needs IV dextrose (a 2 mL/kg D10W bolus, then about 80 mL/kg/day) with a recheck in about 30 minutes; feeding alone is for the asymptomatic infant. Cold stress increases glucose use, so warm her to 36.5-37.5. Draw a blood culture of at least 1 mL, then give ampicillin and gentamicin promptly; a cephalosporin alone misses Listeria.

volume.ask: Why does the culture need at least 1 mL of blood?

choices.label: Smaller volumes can miss bacteria that are there
The lab will reject anything smaller
It doesn't; a few drops is enough

volume.explain: Newborn bacteremia can be low-level; pediatric bottles need about 1 mL for reliable recovery of organisms, so a small sample can give a falsely negative result.

source.cite: Puopolo KM, Benitz WE, Zaoutis TE; AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn, Committee on Infectious Diseases. Management of Neonates Born at >=35 0/7 Weeks' Gestation With Suspected or Proven Early-Onset Bacterial Sepsis. Pediatrics 2018;142(6):e20182894
source.note: Quoted: pediatric bottles 'generally require a minimum inoculum of 1 mL of blood for optimal recovery of organisms.'

listeria.ask: While the IV goes in: why ampicillin plus gentamicin rather than a cephalosporin alone?
listeria.explain: Listeria monocytogenes is resistant to cephalosporins; ampicillin covers it and GBS, and gentamicin adds gram-negative coverage. The AAP names the combination as the first choice for early-onset sepsis.

source.cite: Puopolo KM, Benitz WE, Zaoutis TE; AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn, Committee on Infectious Diseases. Management of Neonates Born at >=35 0/7 Weeks' Gestation With Suspected or Proven Early-Onset Bacterial Sepsis. Pediatrics 2018;142(6):e20182894
source.note: Quoted: 'Ampicillin and gentamicin, in combination, is the first choice for empirical therapy for EOS.' The Listeria point is from the course objective; the report was read for the combination.

ivNotFeed.ask: If this glucose comes back at 31 in a jittery baby who will not feed, what treats it?

choices.label: IV dextrose bolus, then an infusion
A feed and a recheck in an hour

ivNotFeed.explain: IV dextrose. Feeding and a recheck is the plan for an asymptomatic baby; a symptomatic low glucose (jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy) needs IV treatment, a 2-3 mL/kg D10W bolus and then an infusion.
